The research identifies conditions under which stationary solutions exist and analyzes their stability, ultimately classifying the systems behavior into different types based on parameters. Notably, the model exhibits a Turing bifurcation, leading to the formation of spatial patterns. Numerical simulations are used to validate theoretical findings and illustrate the emergence of Turing structures.

This paper introduces a new form of reward manipulation, where an adversary modifies the environment's state through state perturbations, effectively masking their true intentions. This type of deception is particularly insidious because it is based on the attacker's knowledge of the system's underlying dynamics. A new class of deception-driven Markov decision processes is proposed to model this behavior. A new algorithm called RCE is introduced to detect and mitigate deception in this context, using only reward and environment dynamics, without direct access to the attacker's knowledge. RCE leverages the consistency between state perturbations and the underlying dynamics to identify deception, using a detection criterion that can be efficiently computed. Theoretical analysis shows that RCE's detection capability approaches optimal under certain conditions, and experiments demonstrate its superiority over existing methods in identifying deception.

However, the security of smart contracts is often compromised due to coding errors or malicious intent, necessitating the development of a reliable security verification method. This paper proposes a security verification framework for smart contracts that includes a formal language for Rusk, a type of contract suitable for the Rust programming language. The framework includes a compiler that transforms the Rust program into a Rusk contract and then executes the security verification algorithm. This paper presents the design of the formal language, the compiler, and the model-checking algorithm used for Rusk contracts, along with an evaluation of the framework. However, existing GCN approaches struggle to accurately detect community structures in graphs with multiple connections and a high level of noise. To address this challenge, a new approach, Deep Adaptive GCN (DAGCN), is proposed. DAGCN builds upon the GCN framework by incorporating a novel architecture that utilizes multiple sub-networks, each with its own unique role in DAGCN's three-stage process. In the first stage, GCN is employed to extract a basic community structure from the input graph. In the second stage, a new attention mechanism is used to identify and prioritize the most relevant features in each sub-network's output. In the final stage, a novel approach is used to combine the outputs of the sub-networks and produce a more robust and accurate community structure. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world graphs demonstrate the superior performance of DAGCN in detecting community structures, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

General Relativity can be reformulated using a symplectic geometry approach, specifically the Plebanski-Hehl-Datta action. This action is then constrained to a self-dual two-form field with an anti-self-dual conjugate variable, influenced by a topological term and ferromagnetic coupling. Our study shows that these topological and ferromagnetic terms remain relevant in the dual spin network model derived from this lattice theory, as they retain their impact on the boundary conformal field theory. However, in the semiclassical geometry phase of the dual model, the topological term continues to be relevant, but the ferromagnetic term becomes irrelevant.

A key issue is the lack of clarity in understanding how to properly incorporate BRST symmetry into the supersymmetric gauge theories' algebra. This study introduces a novel approach to adS/CFT by utilizing a conformal extension of the superconformal algebra, which has a local gauge-theory counterpart. This method enables a more precise formulation of the N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory with four-component supercharges in four dimensions, and provides a clearer insight into the underlying algebraic structures. Furthermore, this approach is applied to derive a conformal extension of the supergravity algebra, which may have implications for the anti-de Sitter space/gravity duality.

we introduce a new effect, the retrograde Hall effect, where applying a transverse field results in a perpendicular response flowing opposite to the material's perimeter. This occurs due to the unique properties of a two-dimensional, time-reversal symmetric system with a non-trivial topology, causing it to emit chiral edge states. However, when placed on a curved surface, these edge states emit charge in the direction opposite to the applied field, reminiscent of the inverse Chern effect. We demonstrate that the retrograde Hall effect persists at zero temperature and can be understood as a topological version of the Onsager reciprocity principle.

accurately transcribing spoken words into written text. This study leverages a deep neural network framework to achieve a highly precise orthographic alignment between spoken and written language. The proposed alignment system is built upon a neural transducer architecture, enabling it to identify matching sections of phonetic and graphemic representations. The graphemic side is represented using one-to-one character embeddings, while the phonetic side uses one-to-one phone embeddings. Additionally, a sequence of phoneme sequences is represented using a phone bigram context, while a similar mechanism is applied to the character bigram context on the character side. The proposed system was tested on the Switchboard corpus, and the results show that it is capable of accurately aligning spoken and written language.

By analyzing the resulting one-body density matrices of $^{192}\mathrm{Pb}$ across various rotational energies, we calculated their quadrupole moments. Our investigation revealed that these nuclei maintain their distorted halo structure, with rotation causing them to elongate perpendicular to their initial axis. We also determined the radii of these nuclei, finding that their neutron distributions expand significantly in all directions while proton radii remain relatively unaffected. Ultimately, our results illustrate that rotation in these distorted halo nuclei results in their flattening, in contrast to solid deformed nuclei which would split into different shapes depending on their deformation.

In this context, we examine the concept of superpopulation variance for systematic sampling and demonstrate that its value is determined by the sampling interval's variance. This finding is significant as it enables the adjustment of variance estimation formulas to account for variation in the sampling interval. Our analysis also reveals that the Naylor-Wolfe product estimate is equivalent to a variance estimate based on the sampling interval, an insight that has practical implications. Specifically, when the population is arranged in geographically dispersed lists, the variance estimation formulas of Chizema and Lohr can be revised to align with our variance definition for systematic sampling. A common regularization approach is based on a total variation (TV) norm, which is non-smooth and results in solutions with sharp edges. However, these solutions can exhibit excessive blurring and staircasing effects. To address this issue, a new objective function is proposed that uses a fractional $q$-variation ($0 < q < 1$) instead of the TV norm. This new term is shown to have desirable properties such as convexity for $q \geq 1/n$ and lower semi-continuity for $q > 1/2$, making it a suitable alternative to the TV norm. An algorithm is also proposed to solve the new objective function efficiently and a numerical experiment is conducted to demonstrate its effectiveness.

screens, which distort the images of distant celestial bodies. Scientists study these screens to gain insights into the structure of small-scale structures within them. By analyzing the scattering patterns of multiple background sources, researchers can map out the three-dimensional structure of electron density within the screens. This study uses a specific screen known as the Tycho 2 screen, scattering the images of about 200 background sources. To better understand this screen's three-dimensional structure, a new method is proposed that combines a three-dimensional volume mesh with a scattering model, allowing for a more detailed analysis of the screen's features. This method takes advantage of sources with different sizes, allowing researchers to study structures on various scales. The results show that the Tycho 2 screen contains filaments and sheet-like structures, as well as a dense core, which may be responsible for broadening the spectra of pulsars. This study also provides a detailed map of the screen's density profile, which can be used to better understand the effects of interstellar scattering on celestial observations.

The basalts from both volcanoes shared similar isotopic signatures, indicating a common source in the mantle.  The isotopic data revealed that the mantle sources beneath these two volcanoes are laterally interconnected.  The isotopic signatures of the basalts from Karymsky and Bezymianny were compared to those from the 1908 White Earth Lake eruption, which also originated from Kamchatka.  The data from these eruptions provide constraints on the size and location of the mantle plume beneath Kamchatka.  The estimated dimensions of the plume are at least 400 km in diameter and 100 km in depth.  The results also suggest that melt migration from the mantle plume to the crust takes place over a distance of no more than 100 km.

By training a speech-to-X model on a speech dataset annotated with target language written transcripts, the model can effectively translate spoken language into the target language by learning a speech-to-X representation. This study compares the speech-to-X model with a traditional two-step approach and finds that the speech-to-X model achieves superior performance when annotated data is available, but the two-step approach remains more practical when working with existing speech-to-text annotations.

The generators of H_n were originally defined by J. Howie in 1971, and since then, various sets of generators have been introduced. This research builds on earlier work, expressing new generator types in terms of earlier ones and using j-norms to establish relationships between them. The findings of this study lead to the conclusion that unipotent elements and elements of G_n^+ can be identified through characteristics of their factorization into a specific number of tile-translators. This conclusion is first shown for the set of generators introduced by Y. Gao and A. Minasyan in 2019, and then the results are adapted to the other generator set. Additionally, this adaptation provides new proofs for theorems stated by Gao and Minasyan.

This one-by-one generative adversarial network model enables the generation of one-to-one image representations from a single latent vector. Building on this foundation, a one-to-one projection network has been developed to map natural images to their corresponding latent vector representations. This study focuses on optimizing the calculation of these potentials for regions defined by a collection of non-overlapping closed curves. A key feature of these regions is that they may include "handles" or tunnels. To address this, we will first examine the topological characteristics of the curves and the boundary of the region. Then, we will apply an algorithm based on the finite element method to solve a specific boundary value problem. Notably, this problem has the same solution as the volume integral, but can be computed using only boundary and curve information. In contrast, alternative methods require knowledge of the function within the region itself. Moreover, our proposed method can be efficiently parallelized and executed on multiple processors.
